opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the change has been pretty dramatic, honestly. When I first started working in this space, there was a lot of skepticism, and some of it was well-earned. Clinicians had seen a lot of hype, and many of the early tools were developed by people who didn't really understand the clinical workflow. You'd have a model that performed beautifully on a retrospective dataset, but nobody had asked, "Where does this actually fit in a physician's day? What decision does it change?" So there was a sense of, "This is a solution looking for a problem."

What I've seen over the last five to ten years is a shift from skepticism to cautious curiosity, and in some areas real enthusiasm. Part of that is generational. Younger clinicians have grown up with technology and are more comfortable with the idea of a tool that augments their judgment. But a bigger part is that the field has matured. We've learned that we need to bring clinicians in at the very beginning, not hand them a finished product and ask them to trust it. When a radiologist or surgeon helps define the question, helps label the data, and understands the model's limitations, the acceptance is completely different.

There's also been a shift in how we talk about it. Early on there was this narrative of AI replacing radiologists or pathologists, which understandably put people on the defensive. Now the conversation is much more about decision support, about reducing burnout, about giving clinicians back time for the parts of medicine that need a human. That framing matters a lot.

That said, I don't want to overstate it. Trust is still conditional. Clinicians want to know how a model was validated, whether it works on their patient population, and what happens when it's wrong. Explainability, transparency, and prospective evaluation are still huge issues. So I'd say acceptance has grown enormously, but it's an earned acceptance, and those of us building these tools have to keep earning it.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention LLMs or say they have expanded clinicians’ ability to conduct research with data.

fable-5.1.text:
Oh, it's changed enormously. When I started working on this, probably ten or so years ago, you'd walk into a room of radiologists or surgeons and say "machine learning" and there was this real skepticism, almost a defensiveness. A lot of the conversation was framed as "is this going to replace me?" And honestly, some of that was fair, because the early demos were often a model trained on one dataset from one institution that fell apart the moment you moved it somewhere else. Clinicians have very good noses for things that don't generalize, because they live with patient variability every day.

What I've seen shift is that the question has moved from "should we trust this at all" to "where does this fit in my workflow, and how do I know when it's wrong." That's a much more mature conversation. Part of that is just exposure. Younger trainees have grown up with these tools, and they're not intimidated by them. Part of it is that the deployed systems got more honest. Instead of promising to diagnose cancer, the ones that actually stuck were doing things like triaging the worklist, flagging a scan that should be read first, or segmenting a tumour so a surgeon doesn't have to spend forty minutes contouring by hand. Those are boring, but they're the things that earned trust.

I'd also say the pandemic accelerated it. People suddenly had to accept that data and remote tools were going to be part of care, and some of the resistance just evaporated under pressure.

The caveat I'd put on all of that is acceptance isn't uniform. The gap now is less between clinicians who believe and clinicians who don't, and more between institutions that have the infrastructure and governance to deploy responsibly and those that don't. And I think the next five years, the hard part won't be convincing clinicians. It'll be making sure the tools we hand them actually deserve the trust they're now willing to give.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s been a real shift. Five to ten years ago, you often had to start by explaining what AI was and why it might be useful in clinical practice. Now, clinicians are much more familiar with it, and the conversation is more about, “Does this actually work? Does it work for my patients? And how would I use it?”

That familiarity doesn’t necessarily mean trust, though. Clinicians want evidence that a tool improves care, and they need to understand its limitations. If it adds work or gives them a prediction they can’t act on, it’s a hard sell. I think acceptance grows when clinicians are involved in defining the problem and developing the solution—when it’s something that helps them address a real clinical need.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s been a real shift from skepticism to curiosity. Five or ten years ago, a lot of the conversation was about whether AI was going to replace clinicians. Now, the question is much more practical: how can this help me take better care of my patients? Can it reduce some of my workload? Can it give me information that I wouldn’t otherwise have?

But acceptance isn’t the same as trust. Clinicians still want to know that a tool works for their patients, in their setting, and that it fits into their workflow. So I think there’s much more openness now, but we still have to demonstrate that these systems are useful and reliable.
